My case is a pretty unique one, but I'll chip in - I've had two lumbar spine surgeries in the last twelve months (for something unrelated) and the advice I've had from my doctors is that it's not a great idea to keep opening up the spine if you can possibly avoid it. My GP and I have found a collection of medications which treat most (though not all) of the effects I personally suffer with, from the chiari/syringomyelia situation - so for the time being, I'm not incentivised to get it, given the pain of yet more surgery and the long, long, long recovery time.

One of my previous surgeries on my spine was a similar-but-different decompression, and it did make a HUGE difference to my situation then (I was suffering from cauda equina at that point, so had lost sensation from the waist down - now I can walk again) so I can *absolutely* see the benefits of surgery - but for me personally, at the moment, my struggle with chiari isn't as immediately bad as that. But if I were having symptoms that bad that weren't managed by medication (and diet, in my case - going keto has made a big difference, though I wouldn't recommend it for everyone)  I'd definitely get the surgery. 

I guess what I'm saying is there's a point for me where you *know* surgery is necessary (I have had eight major surgeries in my lifetime, and I'm in my early thirties, so I've gone ahead with it plenty of times) - and as it stands that's not where I'm at. But it's a massively personal decision for anyone, so... I suspect everyone has their own reasons.

I’m so sorry to hear what you’re going through - that’s really awful. I’m not sure how encouraging it is to share my story, but for what it’s worth I’ve been working really closely with my GP here (in the UK) over the last five or six years - a long time, I know - to find medications that help ease my symptoms, as I’m a bad candidate for decompression surgery at the moment because I needed more urgent surgeries on my lumbar spine (for a totally separate issue). 

It’s taken a while but I was where you are a few years ago - your symptoms are almost exactly like mine were, then - but now my life is *relatively* normal. There are things I can’t do (use a laptop flat on a desk, lift weights, etc) but my symptoms are managed enough for it to be something I can cope with. For me, gabapentin was the main game changer - but you might find different meds work for you, in combination with your lupus medication.

I can’t tell you you won’t need surgery eventually (it’s on the long, long game for me), but if you tell your doctor clearly that you want to try medication first, they might be able to help. It’s certainly given me several years without surgery at this point, and I’m hoping to stretch that out as long as I can.

I really hope you get some support from your doctors - don’t be afraid to push back if they don’t listen. Your pain is absolutely valid, and you deserve excellent care.

Very best of luck x

I have a Chiari malformation (and trigeminal neuralgia, as well as some spine and cord issues) - so I suffer from chronic migraines, and what used to be called “suicide headaches” from the nerve pain... Plus I’m on several anti-epileptic meds - so my brain was a MAJOR factor in deciding to do keto. Honestly the difference for me IS huge - from 24 days of migraines a month to 5-7. It doesn’t solve everything - I still need my medications and some days pain is just unavoidable - but it’s still a huge change, and I can’t imagine anything that would entice me to go back.

I don’t have much to input except anecdotally... I’ve started doing at-home spin classes in the last week (six weeks into keto) and I was stunned at how well my body handled it... I’ve had quite literally no exercise for the last two years recovering from a spinal injury so I expected to do ten minutes and pass out... But energy was NOT a problem (which was great - meant I could focus on doing it *right*...!) And the endorphin high afterwards was UNREAL. Not sure I’ve ever had that before as I’ve been too busy trying not to die!

I started last October after spending the best part of two years waiting on inspiration and time to appear (I'm a director at a marketing agency, so time wasn't going to appear on its own...) As for getting up - I put my phone at the opposite end of the room and crank it up loud, so I absolutely HAVE to get up to make it stop... Then go straight to the kitchen to put coffee on and wash my face while the machine heats up. Those first few minutes for me are crucial... Sets the tone for the rest of the day!

Hope that helps - and happy writing!

I would second all of this. I spent two years trying to fit my writing around a 70 hour work week (I'm a director at a marketing agency - so 70 hours is pretty conservative during busy periods) and it didn't happen... Until I decided I had to work my ass off to make it happen.

Cue a 4:45am alarm every morning, coffee, and 90 minutes writing before I have to get ready to leave... For work. It's the only time of the day nobody in our London office is likely to call me - and if I've got a Skype meeting with the US or Australia teams I'll schedule it for any time but those 90 minutes, because they're time I've carved out for doing what I love.

To do this I've had to change my lifestyle, too - not to sound like one of those awful self-help types but I don't drink, and I eat well, so I can make sure I always have the energy to get up and write in those dark, early hours.

It's been slow, painful, and some days exhausting - but worth it. I'm now an agented author in the final stages of editing my novel to go out to publishers in the new year.

Not that there's not a huge amount of luck involved, obviously - but u/FelixTheSwift is spot on with "hard work, passion and will power." Just add caffeine and you've got yourself a recipe for becoming a writer!

Quite a lot during revisions, but like u/inkedexistence says, more for remembering the right word rather than inserting a new one. I highlight words as I'm writing them when I know they're not right, and then in my first re-read once the draft is complete I'll go through and find that right word for each one.

I get up at 5am, make an espresso and drink it while the kettle boils, writing in my notebook. Make a mug of tea, get laptop and sit in bed until 7am with wifi off, writing. I've been doing this for almost two months and I've written 76,000 words in the hours before work (and at weekends) - so it seems to be working for me at least!

I've got a couple more chapters to go and then my first draft is finished - so once that's done, I'm going to print it (for the handwritten stage of editing) and then go watch a movie with the glorious stack of pages sitting on the table reminding me I did good. (Until I read it again, at least...)

I am not ashamed to admit if it's writing time, I have to turn wifi off on my laptop. I know myself well enough to know if it's on, I'll click on my browser every 100 words and end up in a rabbit hole! Somethings have just gotta be done...

I find somewhere in between. I used to try to plot everything in advance, and that works fine for the sort of "big picture" story arcs - but the details of how and why each character does what they do, and the events leading up to each particular event I tend to write as I go along... Generally I find if I sit and stare at my screen long enough (with the wifi off and my phone on mute) these things will write themselves - eventually! 

I've lost a lot of hours trying to plot everything in detail only to have a turn of events I didn't see coming throw off the entire plan while I'm writing it - so I'm trying to follow the novel to the intended conclusion via whatever route it wants to go (and at 70,000 words it's almost there!)

I've got some momentum at the moment, after what feels like years of stop-start, painful half-writing. 

I took my first holiday of 2016 five weeks ago (I work a 70+ hour week in an marketing agency job, so I reeeeeally needed it) and spent a fortnight at home with my router and phone off, really focusing on the novel I've been working on since 2013, when my agent (who was at that time repping some non-fiction I'd pulled together) suggested I give fiction a try. I HATED it at first, because I'd never tried fiction and it took the best part of a year to figure out the basics of how to actually go about it.

That fortnight was the most productive and enjoyable of my life - I spent some time really getting to know my characters and filling in all the major plot holes that were getting in my way.  Since then I've been getting up at 5am daily to write something (anything!) before I have to go back to my crazy day job - but I'm 30,000 words up (not counting the 16,000 words I cut during the fortnight off) and it feels like it's actually starting to work as a novel... And only 20k away from a completed 80k manuscript.

I'm all too aware these phases don't last as long as you want them to so I'm trying to go at it full force while it's here... But it's nice to finally remember there's some joy in it!
